## Abstract

[](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462)
The origins of money and the formulation of coherent weight and measurement systems are amongst the most significant prehistoric developments of the human intellect. We present a method for detecting perceptible standardization of weights and apply this to 5028 Early Bronze Age rings, ribs, and axe blades from Central Europe. We calculate the degree of uniformity on the basis of psychophysics, and quantify this using similarity indexes. The analysis shows that 70.3% of all rings could not be perceptibly distinguished from a ring weighing 195.5 grams, indicating their suitability as commodity money. Perceptive weight equivalence is demonstrated between rings, and a selection of ribs and axe blades. Co-occurrence of these objects evidences their interchangeability. We further suggest that producing copies of rings led to recognition of weight similarities and the independent emergence of a system of weighing in Central Europe at the end of the Early Bronze Age.

[](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462 "Introduction")
## Introduction

[](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462)
Money is a type of commodity that acts as a means of exchange and is standardized to some degree, visually or in terms of their weight [[1](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref001), [2](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref002)]. Archaeology can provide a unique perspective on the development of money and systems of weighing over space and time, but the discipline has difficulties with the identification of objects that functioned either as commodity money or as (balance) weights. Typical statistical approaches are inadequate for dealing with the approximation that characterizes prehistoric weighing [[3](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref003), [4](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref004)]. What is needed for archaeology to contribute to the history of metrology and the origins of money are methods for identifying standardization on the basis of perceived similarity. A principal challenge at this point is to take the statistical tools employed to express accuracy, and adjust them in accordance to the findings from psychophysics, so that the ordinal and qualitative measurements of weight estimation by hand and sight are taken on board. In short, prehistoric weight units quite literally need to make sense.

[](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462 "Bronze Age commodities")
### Bronze Age commodities

[](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462)
Commodities are archaeologically defined as socially recognized, alienable objects that appear in large numbers and emphasize similarity [[5](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref005)–[9](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref009)]. Candidates of prehistoric commodity money from the Central European Early Bronze Age are the so-called _Ösenringe_ (hereafter rings), _Spangenbarren_ (hereafter ribs), and possibly axe blades. Rings and ribs appear in the southern parts of Central Europe: the Danubian region of southern Germany, Lower Austria, and parts of the Czech Republic. Axe blades are typically, but not exclusively, found in central and north-eastern Germany, roughly corresponding to the cultural area of the Únětice. In between is an area of overlap where rings, ribs, and axe blades are regularly found together, primarily the Czech Republic (Moravia and Bohemia), though some mixed hoards also appear in north-eastern Germany and Poland ([Fig 1](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone-0240462-g001)). A third geographical region where these objects are encountered is Southern Scandinavia, though in lesser numbers [[10](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref010)] ([S1A Appendix](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.s001)).

[](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462)

[![Image 13: thumbnail](link_15)](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article/figure/image?size=medium&id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462.g001 [link_20] "Click for larger image")

[](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462)

Includes drawings of objects after Stein [[11](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref011)] (made with Natural Earth).

[https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0240462.g001](link_23)

[](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462)
It is generally thought that different economies operated in the three regions where rings, ribs, and axe blades occur [[10](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref010)]. In the southern region commodification was strongest and the economy is often interpreted as resembling to some degree a market economy, in which rings and ribs represented wealth [[12](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref012)–[15](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref015)]. The Únětice region is better characterized as prestige-good exchange, though some commodification is visible [[14](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref014)]. Scandinavia is different altogether. Here the context of rings suggests gift-exchange, and they mostly appear deposited as single finds in wetlands [[10](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref010)]. A clear contrast between gift and market economies seems hard to sustain, however, and may be little more than a modern distinction [[5](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref005), [10](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref010), [16](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref016)].

[](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462)
Found in bulk, sometimes in hoards containing multiple hundreds, many of the rings, ribs and axe blades are considered to have no other practical function besides their tentative use as ingots, or rough-outs for further production [[8](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref008), [17](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref017)–[23](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref023)]. Moulds, made of clay, stone, or casted directly in sand [[24](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref024)], made serial production possible, which led to some degree of unintentional standardization. However, there are indications that for some types of objects a deliberate effort was made to achieve a specific weight interval, meaning that weight mattered ([S1A Appendix](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.s001)). In the case of rings, a standardization between roughly 170 and 220 grams has been hypothesized on the basis of histograms [[17](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref017)–[19](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref019)]. Unclear is how prehistoric people would have recognized this standard.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7816976/)Abstract

The origins of money and the formulation of coherent weight and measurement systems are amongst the most significant prehistoric developments of the human intellect. We present a method for detecting perceptible standardization of weights and apply this to 5028 Early Bronze Age rings, ribs, and axe blades from Central Europe. We calculate the degree of uniformity on the basis of psychophysics, and quantify this using similarity indexes. The analysis shows that 70.3% of all rings could not be perceptibly distinguished from a ring weighing 195.5 grams, indicating their suitability as commodity money. Perceptive weight equivalence is demonstrated between rings, and a selection of ribs and axe blades. Co-occurrence of these objects evidences their interchangeability. We further suggest that producing copies of rings led to recognition of weight similarities and the independent emergence of a system of weighing in Central Europe at the end of the Early Bronze Age.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7816976/)Introduction

Money is a type of commodity that acts as a means of exchange and is standardized to some degree, visually or in terms of their weight [[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7816976/#pone.0240462.ref001), [2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7816976/#pone.0240462.ref002)]. Archaeology can provide a unique perspective on the development of money and systems of weighing over space and time, but the discipline has difficulties with the identification of objects that functioned either as commodity money or as (balance) weights. Typical statistical approaches are inadequate for dealing with the approximation that characterizes prehistoric weighing [[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7816976/#pone.0240462.ref003), [4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7816976/#pone.0240462.ref004)]. What is needed for archaeology to contribute to the history of metrology and the origins of money are methods for identifying standardization on the basis of perceived similarity. A principal challenge at this point is to take the statistical tools employed to express accuracy, and adjust them in accordance to the findings from psychophysics, so that the ordinal and qualitative measurements of weight estimation by hand and sight are taken on board. In short, prehistoric weight units quite literally need to make sense.

### Bronze Age commodities

Commodities are archaeologically defined as socially recognized, alienable objects that appear in large numbers and emphasize similarity [[5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7816976/#pone.0240462.ref005)–[9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7816976/#pone.0240462.ref009)]. Candidates of prehistoric commodity money from the Central European Early Bronze Age are the so-called _Ösenringe_ (hereafter rings), _Spangenbarren_ (hereafter ribs), and possibly axe blades. Rings and ribs appear in the southern parts of Central Europe: the Danubian region of southern Germany, Lower Austria, and parts of the Czech Republic. Axe blades are typically, but not exclusively, found in central and north-eastern Germany, roughly corresponding to the cultural area of the Únětice. In between is an area of overlap where rings, ribs, and axe blades are regularly found together, primarily the Czech Republic (Moravia and Bohemia), though some mixed hoards also appear in north-eastern Germany and Poland ([Fig 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7816976/#pone.0240462.g001)). A third geographical region where these objects are encountered is Southern Scandinavia, though in lesser numbers [[10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7816976/#pone.0240462.ref010)] ([S1A Appendix](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7816976/#pone.0240462.s001)).

Fig 1. Map of Central Europe with the hoards used in this study.
[![Image 15: Fig 1](https://pmc-oa-opendata.s3.amazonaws.com/PMC7816976.1/pone.0240462.g001.jpg)](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/core/lw/2.0/html/tileshop_pmc/tileshop_pmc_inline.html?title=Click%20on%20image%20to%20zoom&p=PMC3&id=7816976_pone.0240462.g001.jpg)

[Open in a new tab](link_19)

Includes drawings of objects after Stein [[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7816976/#pone.0240462.ref011)] (made with Natural Earth).

It is generally thought that different economies operated in the three regions where rings, ribs, and axe blades occur [[10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7816976/#pone.0240462.ref010)]. In the southern region commodification was strongest and the economy is often interpreted as resembling to some degree a market economy, in which rings and ribs represented wealth [[12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7816976/#pone.0240462.ref012)–[15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7816976/#pone.0240462.ref015)]. The Únětice region is better characterized as prestige-good exchange, though some commodification is visible [[14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7816976/#pone.0240462.ref014)]. Scandinavia is different altogether. Here the context of rings suggests gift-exchange, and they mostly appear deposited as single finds in wetlands [[10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7816976/#pone.0240462.ref010)]. A clear contrast between gift and market economies seems hard to sustain, however, and may be little more than a modern distinction [[5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7816976/#pone.0240462.ref005), [10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7816976/#pone.0240462.ref010), [16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7816976/#pone.0240462.ref016)].

Found in bulk, sometimes in hoards containing multiple hundreds, many of the rings, ribs and axe blades are considered to have no other practical function besides their tentative use as ingots, or rough-outs for further production [[8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7816976/#pone.0240462.ref008), [17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7816976/#pone.0240462.ref017)–[23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7816976/#pone.0240462.ref023)]. Moulds, made of clay, stone, or casted directly in sand [[24](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7816976/#pone.0240462.ref024)], made serial production possible, which led to some degree of unintentional standardization. However, there are indications that for some types of objects a deliberate effort was made to achieve a specific weight interval, meaning that weight mattered ([S1A Appendix](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7816976/#pone.0240462.s001)). In the case of rings, a standardization between roughly 170 and 220 grams has been hypothesized on the basis of histograms [[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7816976/#pone.0240462.ref017)–[19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7816976/#pone.0240462.ref019)]. Unclear is how prehistoric people would have recognized this standard.

### Psychophysics of weight discrimination

The practice of weighing may have been far more imprecise than is generally assumed. According to Gyllenbok [[25](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7816976/#pone.0240462.ref025)], historically there are three basic ways to measure weight: 1) Through lifting two objects and comparing them, or estimation on sight. 2) Through practicality, i.e. the maximum weight that could be conveniently carried by a human or animal. 3) By means of a weighing apparatus. Each of these have their own level of impreciseness.

In the case of the Central European Early Bronze Age, there is no evidence of a weighing apparatus such as balances. Weighing was a qualitative measurement based on comparative sensory perception with hands and eyes. But humans are known to be “rather ‘noisy’ measurement instruments” [[26](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7816976/#pone.0240462.ref026)]. Prehistoric standardization thus would have been imprecise, and worked based on approximation both in shape and weight. They must have had relatively low precision in terms of modern scientific tolerances [[25](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7816976/#pone.0240462.ref025)] and this should be taken into consideration when looking for standardization.

We assume that in the absence of measuring equipment counting must have been the preferred method of quantification, but the counted objects had to be perceptibly similar [[25](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7816976/#pone.0240462.ref025), [27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7816976/#pone.0240462.ref027), [28](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7816976/#pone.0240462.ref028)]. Therefore, weight mattered. Weight is crucial for the determination of the value of goods in most economic transactions [[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7816976/#pone.0240462.ref003)]. Lacking balances, the only way to observe a reasonable degree of uniformity is through sensory perception. We consider objects uniform when they are perceptibly indiscriminate from each other.

Psychophysics offers a methodology through which we can test the perceptible similarity of objects based on weight. This sub-field of cognitive psychology is concerned with the relationships between physical properties of stimuli and perceptual responses to these stimuli [[29](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7816976/#pone.0240462.ref029)–[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7816976/#pone.0240462.ref031)]. The measure used to express people’s sensory acuity is the Weber fraction, and denotes the difference in stimulus strength that is just noticeable. As a general rule, the Weber fraction for weight discrimination is 0.1 [[32](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7816976/#pone.0240462.ref032)–[34](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7816976/#pone.0240462.ref034)]. This means that the difference between, for example, a weight of 100 grams and 105 grams is not noticeable, but between 100 and 111 grams is, since the threshold is at 110 grams ([Methods](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7816976/#sec011)).

### Data

Using the measurement of weight, we employ a methodology based on psychophysics to quantify and operationalize our assumption that weighing in prehistory was a purely sensorial practice, done by hand. The perceptive equivalence is expressed though the calculation of a similarity index (SI), which gives the percentage of objects from a dataset that are perceptibly indistinguishable from a tested object ([Methods](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7816976/#sec011)).

We collected the weights of 6317 objects, of which 5028 were used in the analysis as they were complete and dated to the Early Bronze Age: 2639 rings, 1780 ribs, and 609 axe blades ([S2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7816976/#pone.0240462.s002) and [S3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7816976/#pone.0240462.s003) Appendices). Axe blades can be divided into Early Bronze I (hereafter: EBA I: 2150–1900 BCE) and Early Bronze Age II (hereafter EBA II: 1900–1700 BCE) on typological grounds [[35](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7816976/#pone.0240462.ref035), [36](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7816976/#pone.0240462.ref036)]. Rings and ribs mostly overlap, though ribs are generally considered a slightly later development [[18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7816976/#pone.0240462.ref018)].

## Abstract

[](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0240462)
The origins of money and the formulation of coherent weight and measurement systems are amongst the most significant prehistoric developments of the human intellect. We present a method for detecting perceptible standardization of weights and apply this to 5028 Early Bronze Age rings, ribs, and axe blades from Central Europe. We calculate the degree of uniformity on the basis of psychophysics, and quantify this using similarity indexes. The analysis shows that 70.3% of all rings could not be perceptibly distinguished from a ring weighing 195.5 grams, indicating their suitability as commodity money. Perceptive weight equivalence is demonstrated between rings, and a selection of ribs and axe blades. Co-occurrence of these objects evidences their interchangeability. We further suggest that producing copies of rings led to recognition of weight similarities and the independent emergence of a system of weighing in Central Europe at the end of the Early Bronze Age.

**Citation:**Kuijpers MHG, Popa CN (2021) The origins of money: Calculation of similarity indexes demonstrates the earliest development of commodity money in prehistoric Central Europe. PLoS ONE 16(1): e0240462. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0240462

[](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0240462 "Introduction")
## Introduction

[](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0240462)
Money is a type of commodity that acts as a means of exchange and is standardized to some degree, visually or in terms of their weight [[1](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref001), [2](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref002)]. Archaeology can provide a unique perspective on the development of money and systems of weighing over space and time, but the discipline has difficulties with the identification of objects that functioned either as commodity money or as (balance) weights. Typical statistical approaches are inadequate for dealing with the approximation that characterizes prehistoric weighing [[3](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref003), [4](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref004)]. What is needed for archaeology to contribute to the history of metrology and the origins of money are methods for identifying standardization on the basis of perceived similarity. A principal challenge at this point is to take the statistical tools employed to express accuracy, and adjust them in accordance to the findings from psychophysics, so that the ordinal and qualitative measurements of weight estimation by hand and sight are taken on board. In short, prehistoric weight units quite literally need to make sense.

[](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0240462 "Bronze Age commodities")
### Bronze Age commodities

[](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0240462)
Commodities are archaeologically defined as socially recognized, alienable objects that appear in large numbers and emphasize similarity [[5](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref005)–[9](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref009)]. Candidates of prehistoric commodity money from the Central European Early Bronze Age are the so-called _Ösenringe_ (hereafter rings), _Spangenbarren_ (hereafter ribs), and possibly axe blades. Rings and ribs appear in the southern parts of Central Europe: the Danubian region of southern Germany, Lower Austria, and parts of the Czech Republic. Axe blades are typically, but not exclusively, found in central and north-eastern Germany, roughly corresponding to the cultural area of the Únětice. In between is an area of overlap where rings, ribs, and axe blades are regularly found together, primarily the Czech Republic (Moravia and Bohemia), though some mixed hoards also appear in north-eastern Germany and Poland ([Fig 1](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone-0240462-g001)). A third geographical region where these objects are encountered is Southern Scandinavia, though in lesser numbers [[10](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref010)] ([S1A Appendix](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.s001)).

[](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0240462)

[![Image 8: thumbnail](link_58)](https://doi.org/10.1371/article/figure/image?size=medium&id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462.g001 [link_59] "Click for larger image")

 Download: 
*   [PNG larger image](link_60)
*   [TIFF original image](link_61)

Fig 1.  Map of Central Europe with the hoards used in this study.

[](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0240462)

Includes drawings of objects after Stein [[11](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref011)] (made with Natural Earth).

[https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0240462.g001](link_62)

[](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0240462)
It is generally thought that different economies operated in the three regions where rings, ribs, and axe blades occur [[10](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref010)]. In the southern region commodification was strongest and the economy is often interpreted as resembling to some degree a market economy, in which rings and ribs represented wealth [[12](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref012)–[15](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref015)]. The Únětice region is better characterized as prestige-good exchange, though some commodification is visible [[14](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref014)]. Scandinavia is different altogether. Here the context of rings suggests gift-exchange, and they mostly appear deposited as single finds in wetlands [[10](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref010)]. A clear contrast between gift and market economies seems hard to sustain, however, and may be little more than a modern distinction [[5](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref005), [10](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref010), [16](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref016)].

[](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0240462)
Found in bulk, sometimes in hoards containing multiple hundreds, many of the rings, ribs and axe blades are considered to have no other practical function besides their tentative use as ingots, or rough-outs for further production [[8](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref008), [17](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref017)–[23](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref023)]. Moulds, made of clay, stone, or casted directly in sand [[24](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref024)], made serial production possible, which led to some degree of unintentional standardization. However, there are indications that for some types of objects a deliberate effort was made to achieve a specific weight interval, meaning that weight mattered ([S1A Appendix](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.s001)). In the case of rings, a standardization between roughly 170 and 220 grams has been hypothesized on the basis of histograms [[17](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref017)–[19](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref019)]. Unclear is how prehistoric people would have recognized this standard.

[](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0240462 "Psychophysics of weight discrimination")
### Psychophysics of weight discrimination

[](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0240462)
The practice of weighing may have been far more imprecise than is generally assumed. According to Gyllenbok [[25](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref025)], historically there are three basic ways to measure weight: 1) Through lifting two objects and comparing them, or estimation on sight. 2) Through practicality, i.e. the maximum weight that could be conveniently carried by a human or animal. 3) By means of a weighing apparatus. Each of these have their own level of impreciseness.

[](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0240462)
In the case of the Central European Early Bronze Age, there is no evidence of a weighing apparatus such as balances. Weighing was a qualitative measurement based on comparative

## Abstract

The Bell Beaker bracers, or wrist-guards, are traditionally thought to have functioned as archery equipment, protecting the arm against the sting of the bowstring. Their position on the body is therefore thought to have been on the inside of the lower arm. Through analysis of the position in which wrist-guards are found, we have come to the conclusion that they were, however, more often than not fastened to the outside of the arm, which leads us to consider a range of new possible uses and meanings for the bracers. With combined information from archaeological and ethnographic surveys we have come to think of the stone wrist-guard as an artefact that was associated with a martial, ideologically-laden activity in the Bell Beaker culture.

* * *

## Résumé

On considérait traditionnellement que les brassards, ou protège-poignets, fonctionnaient comme équipement pour le tir à l'arc, protégeant le bras contre le frottement de la corde. On pensait donc qu'ils étaient placés sur le corps à l'intérieur de la partie inférieure du bras. A la suite à l'analyse de la position dans laquelle on a retrouvé ces protège-poignets, nous sommes arrivés à la conclusion que, toutefois, ils n'étaient le plus souvent pas attachés à l'extérieur du bras, ce qui nous conduit à envisager une gamme de nouvelles utilisations et significations possibles pour ces brassards. Rassemblant les renseignements d'études archéologiques et ethnographiques, nous en sommes venus à considérer le protège-poignet en pierre comme un objet façonné qui était associé à une activité martiale, chargée idéologiquement, de la culture des campaniformes.

* * *

## Zusammenfassung

Der Glockenbecher Armschutz oder Armschutzplatten werden traditionell als Ausrüstung von Bogenschützen interpretiert, die den Arm vor dem Zurückschnellen der Bogensehne schützte. Aus diesem Grund wurde immer davon ausgegangen, dass sie auf der Innenseite des Unterarms getragen wurden. Nach unserer Analyse der Position, an der sie am Körper gefunden wurden, können wir zusammenfassen, dass sie aber öfters an der Außenseite des Arms angebracht waren als an der Innenseite. Daraus schließen wir, dass man eine Reihe von neuen Nutzungsmöglichkeiten und Bedeutungen der Armschutzplatten in Betracht ziehen muss. Auf der Grundlage der Kombination von archäologischen und ethnographischen Untersuchungen sehen wir die Armschutzplatten als ein Artefakt, das mit einem kriegerischen und ideologiegeladenen Tätigkeitsbereich in der Glockenbecher Kultur zusammen hängt.

* * *

## Résumen

Tradicionalmente se explican las brazaleras o pulidores campaniformes como parte del equipo del arquero, con una función protectora del brazo contra la cuerda del arco. Se piensa, por tanto, que su posición en el cuerpo estaba en la parte interna de la parte inferior del brazo. Sin embargo, a través del análisis de la posición en la que se han encontrado los pulidores, hemos llegado a la conclusión de que muy a menudo eran colocados en la parte exterior del brazo, lo que nos lleva a considerar una serie de posibles nuevos usos y significados para estas brazaleras. Combinando la información de estudios arqueológicos y etnográficos hemos interpretado los pulidores de piedra como un artefacto asociado con una actividad marcial y cargada de ideología de la cultura campaniforme.

07/15/2026

New animal species

## [Likweli: A remarkable new species of Colobus monkey from the Lomami National Park, Democratic Republic of Congo](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0349857)

Hart and colleagues discover and describe a new African monkey species Colobus Congoensis in Democratic Republic of Congo, which are also called by the locals "likweli". These monkeys were initially sighted in 2008. living in high tree canopy, they can be recognized by a clear orange color patch around their mouths and noses.

Image credit: [figure a](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0349857) by Hart et al., [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)

[![Image 2: Likweli: A remarkable new species of Colobus monkey from the Lomami National Park, Democratic Republic of Congo](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/indirect/e85f4c6645e52a3cb1bf4daaa1ecf38f76af49386e86961f55da8b61f7052757)](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0349857)

06/18/2026

Dendrogeomorphology

## [Tree ring segmentation performance in highly disturbed trees using deep learning](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0321841)

Zambrano-Suárez and colleagues systematically evaluate the effectiveness of different deep-learning models for tree ring segmentation in increment cores taken from trees with disturbed growth conditions. The study achieves good performance whilst highlighting limits influenced by tissue alterations and image resolution.

Image credit: [tops-of-pine-trees](https://www.publicdomainpictures.net/en/view-image.php?image=117051&picture=tops-of-pine-trees) by Ken Kistler, [CC BY 0](https://www.publicdomainpictures.net/en/terms-of-service.php)

[![Image 3: Tree ring segmentation performance in highly disturbed trees using deep learning](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/indirect/15dd0fedd392f39ce312dc9df7d3110e486cd50f9eb63190a8fc8eb5a4694479)](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0321841)

07/20/2026

Memory/health

## [Autobiographical memory of validating and invalidating consultations is associated with recall capacity for health information](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0353615)

Lee and colleagues find that patients who recall validating healthcare experiences demonstrate better recall of health-related messages. This suggests clinician-validation may play a role in supporting cognitive function for patients with chronic pain.

Image credit: [treatment-hospital-clinic-medicine](https://pixabay.com/photos/treatment-hospital-clinic-medicine-4099432/) by fernandozhiminaicela, [cc by 0](https://pixabay.com/service/terms/)

[![Image 4: Autobiographical memory of validating and invalidating consultations is associated with recall capacity for health information](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/indirect/c39131d8f3a060c4796f523bdd230bc201235b513511976b63f18347a70c5b11)](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0353615)

07/31/2026

Antiretroviral therapy

## [Mixed feelings: Unintended consequences of HIV outreach care in Zimbabwe](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0354747)

Noa Gluskinos and colleagues show that while decentralizing HIV care and expanding antiretroviral therapy (ART) outreach in rural Zimbabwe improves access to treatment, it can also create unintended challenges related to stigma, privacy concerns, and community dynamics, underscoring the need for HIV services that are both accessible and socially supportive.

Image credit: [chemistry-crown-coronavirus-cure](https://pixabay.com/photos/chemistry-crown-coronavirus-cure-4932622/) by padrinan, [CC BY 0](https://pixabay.com/service/terms/)

[![Image 5: Mixed feelings: Unintended consequences of HIV outreach care in Zimbabwe](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/indirect/a1a8441120e2a5f091ef471f7a2a4305f389cf60b75b21556952ca90235b96de)](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0354747)

07/21/2026

EveryOne

## [From long-term field studies to wild microbiomes: themes from Evolution x Ecology 2026](https://everyone.plos.org/2026/07/21/from-long-term-field-studies-to-wild-microbiomes-themes-from-evolution-x-ecology-2026/)

Associate Editor Sarah Jose attended Evolution x Ecology 2026, where researchers discussed how long term studies, open science and collaboration are advancing evolutionary ecology. Key themes included climate change, ageing, host-parasite dynamics, behaviour and the influence of wild microbiomes on adaptation.

[![Image 6: From long-term field studies to wild microbiomes: themes from Evolution x Ecology 2026](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/indirect/19e2dec6ca21aedb6f2bd3c0ee8d0e2af384c11cf9907ada586ced7724cdad5c)](https://everyone.plos.org/2026/07/21/from-long-term-field-studies-to-wild-microbiomes-themes-from-evolution-x-ecology-2026/)
Image credit: [figure a](https://everyone.plos.org/2026/07/21/from-long-term-field-studies-to-wild-microbiomes-themes-from-evolution-x-ecology-2026/) by PLOS et al., [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)

07/10/2026

EveryOne

## [Connection and Collaboration at EACR 2026](https://everyone.plos.org/2026/07/10/connection-and-collaboration-at-eacr-2026/)

Senior Editor Jenny Tucker attended EACR 2026 in Budapest, where cancer researchers highlighted the importance of patient involvement, collaboration and translational research. Discussions covered cancer prevention, biomarkers, tumour biology, personalised therapies and the growing role of open science in accelerating progress.

[![Image 7: Connection and Collaboration at EACR 2026](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/indirect/a6a03d4e839f6479ecb942f776a1a69968e08a02c28f1516fbc90bc60ace6c25)](https://everyone.plos.org/2026/07/10/connection-and-collaboration-at-eacr-2026/)
Image credit: [figure a](https://everyone.plos.org/2026/07/10/connection-and-collaboration-at-eacr-2026/) by PLOS., [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)

06/19/2026

EveryOne

## [Editorial Spotlight: Chen Ling](https://everyone.plos.org/2026/06/19/editorial-spotlight-chen-ling/)

Academic Editor Chen Ling, a Principal Investigator at Fudan University, discusses his work in gene therapy and virology, including advances in gene expression control and AAV research. He also shares his approach to handling manuscripts and offers advice for authors submitting to PLOS ONE.

[![Image 8: Editorial Spotlight: Chen Ling](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/indirect/9910fbd8c8e8ecbea499e5a12123b652c05d9d518ae0caa160a9138e93ffd5e2)](https://everyone.plos.org/2026/06/19/editorial-spotlight-chen-ling/)
Image credit: [figure ar](https://everyone.plos.org/2026/06/19/editorial-spotlight-chen-ling/) by PLOS., [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)

07/17/2026

autism

## [Between neuroaffirmation and access: Parents’ experiences of autism caregiving in England](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0353994)

Farooq and colleagues find that neuroaffirmation is important for some carers of autistic children. Linguistic and cultural differences also shape caregiving roles and expectations.

[![Image 9: Between neuroaffirmation and access: Parents’ experiences of autism caregiving in England](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/indirect/80c89be619d3d9bd01f598618b0d580ac7a16bd11fa6901a6992790c0a09c716)](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0353994)
Image credit: [adult-mother-daughter-beach-kids](https://pixabay.com/photos/adult-mother-daughter-beach-kids-1807500/) by sasint, [CC by 0](https://pixabay.com/service/terms/)

07/31/2026

Aging

## [Task-specific step training for improved balance recovery in community-dwelling older adults](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0354677)

Lee and colleagues' pilot study found that a low-resource training method improved balance recovery after trips in older adults and could be effective in community centers.

[![Image 10: Task-specific step training for improved balance recovery in community-dwelling older adults](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/indirect/b0688a66124c037e457104a5299804e747c72e87dea340c009a47855aeca3d9e)](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0354677)
Image credit: [couple-elderly-walking-fall-trail](https://pixabay.com/photos/couple-elderly-walking-fall-trail-6653517/) by EddieKphoto, [CC by 0](https://pixabay.com/service/terms/)

07/21/2026

Agriculture

## [Comparative evaluation of major cropping patterns in coastal saline-alkali lands](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0353467)

A two-year study by Hongliang Ma and colleagues found that rice rotations with peas, wheat, or crabs reduced pesticide use, nutrient loss, and soil salinity while improving soil quality and farm income.

[![Image 11: Comparative evaluation of major cropping patterns in coastal saline-alkali lands](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/indirect/b6c84586b92871313b2715871301fcc8f2197c65edf04365fd76687d3a60ff7a)](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0353467)
Image credit: [crop-usd-paddy-field-grain-harvest](https://pixabay.com/photos/crop-usd-paddy-field-grain-harvest-5582141/) by Kanenori, [CC by 0](https://pixabay.com/service/terms/)

06/03/2026

Ecology

## [Integrating satellite and field data to predict bird communities in the Amazon](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0329343)

In the Peruvian Amazon, Slater and colleagues found that combining satellite data and field surveys may improve bird distribution predictions, although survey design and detectability remain limitations.

[![Image 12: Integrating satellite and field data to predict bird communities in the Amazon](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/indirect/47a1102eb3115367072a668e6f6dcc9f0373afa33273f7195ecae3e293f44424)](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0329343)

# **Research journals**

## Put integrity first by choosing a PLOS journal

When it comes to research integrity and scientific rigor, we will not compromise. With a focus on fundamental and applied research, our journals cover all scientific disciplines across life, health, and sustainability. We have processes to ensure the science is rigorous, practices to make sure research is shared and reused, policies that are equitable, and innovations in scholarly communications. Our [publication metrics](https://plos.org/metrics/) speak to our commitment to transparency and serving the research community.

Our journals are not just a publ ication venue—we are y our partner in progress. With expert editorial support, transparent processes, and open science tools, we make sure your research gets [the visibility and recognition](https://explore.plos.org/why-publish-with-us) it deserves.

Explore our journals, each publishing research in these scientific disciplines, below.

### [Life science](https://plos.org/our-journals/#life-science)

### [Health science](https://plos.org/our-journals/#health-science)

### [Sustainability science](https://plos.org/our-journals/#sustainability-science)

## Life science

![Image 2: PLOS Biology](https://plos.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/Journal-Three-Column-Ribbon-470x235_Biology.jpg)

### [PLOS Biology](https://journals.plos.org/plosbiology/)

Our leading life science journal,_PLOS Biology,_ champions inclusive, high-impact research across all disciplines—from molecules to ecosystems. We offer innovative publication formats, rigorous, transparent and accountable decision-making, and collaborative editorial support that is focused on helping researchers publish their best work. Our transdisciplinary approach and author-friendly policies ensure your work reaches its full potential and impact.

![Image 3: PLOS Complex Systems](https://plos.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/Journal-Three-Column-Ribbon-470x235_Complex-Systems.jpg)

### [PLOS Complex Systems](https://journals.plos.org/complexsystems/)

_PLOS Complex Systems_ brings together researchers across disciplines, providing a platform for theoretical, modeling, and applied research that advances our understanding of complex systems. The journal encompasses diverse topics—from chaotic systems and networks to risk modeling, systems biology, and economics—emphasizing methodological rigor and broad community impact.

![Image 4: PLOS Computational Biology](https://plos.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/Journal-Three-Column-Ribbon-470x235_CB.jpg)

### [PLOS Computational Biology](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/)

_PLOS Computational Biology_ provides a home for research of exceptional significance that uses computational methods and AI to further our understanding of living systems from molecular to ecosystem scales. We strengthen the accessibility and reusability of your work to empower biologists everywhere.

![Image 5: PLOS Genetics](https://plos.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/Journal-Three-Column-Ribbon-470x235_Genetics.jpg)

### [PLOS Genetics](https://journals.plos.org/plosgenetics/)

_PLOS Genetics_ publishes research related to genetics and genomics across the full breadth of this field, from microbes to humans and from basic science to translational approaches. We welcome cross-disciplinary research that provides new insights and substantially advances our understanding of biological principles and processes. We act as a forum for practicing scientists by publishing high-quality, peer-reviewed research, reviews and opinion articles.

![Image 6: PLOS One](https://plos.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/Journal-Three-Column-Ribbon-470x235_One.jpg)

### [PLOS One](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/)

_PLOS One_ accepts research in over two hundred subject areas across science, engineering, medicine, and the related social sciences and humanities. We evaluate research on the basis of scientific validity, strong methodology, and high ethical standards, selecting for research that contributes to academic knowledge. We encourage inter-and multidisciplinary studies, and accept a range of submissions from primary research to protocols and systematic reviews, including research with negative or null results.

![Image 7: PLOS Pathogens](https://plos.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/Journal-Three-Column-Ribbon-470x235_Pathogens.jpg)

### [PLOS Pathogens](https://journals.plos.org/plospathogens/)

_PLOS Pathogens_ publishes ground-breaking research on pathogen biology and host-pathogen interactions across all life forms. From fundamental discovery through to translational, applied and clinical research we uphold the highest standards of quality, ethics, integrity, and editorial judgment through fair and transparent peer review. Our rigorous selection process ensures that only impactful and high-quality research is published. We are committed to advancing open science and a diverse and inclusive culture that represents our global community and engages with international experts as authors, editors, and reviewers from across the world.

## Health science

![Image 8: PLOS Aging and Health journal image](https://plos.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/Journal-Three-Column-Ribbon-470x235-Aging-Health-AH.jpg)

### [PLOS Aging and Health](https://journals.plos.org/agingandhealth/)

_PLOS Aging and Health_ is an open access journal that publishes transformative work from researchers, clinicians, public health scientists, social scientists, and policymakers across the spectrum of aging research. This selective journal publishes ethical, impactful, immediately accessible research that advances our understanding of aging by integrating biological, developmental, clinical, neurological, and functional dimensions.

![Image 9: PLOS Complex Systems](https://plos.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/Journal-Three-Column-Ribbon-470x235_Complex-Systems.jpg)

### [PLOS Complex Systems](https://journals.plos.org/complexsystems/)

The journal encompasses diverse topics—from chaotic systems and networks to risk modeling, systems biology, and economics—emphasizing methodological rigor and broad community impact.

![Image 10: PLOS Digital Health](https://plos.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/Journal-Three-Column-Ribbon-470x235_Digital-Health.jpg)

### [PLOS Digital Health](https://journals.plos.org/digitalhealth/)

_PLOS Digital Health_ is a journal for democratizing healthcare in the interdisciplinary and digital age. We encourage excellent research from healthcare professionals, policy makers, and other stakeholders across digital health that embraces open code and data sharing to improve health outcomes for patients. We empower researchers to ensure that progress and technology in this rapidly-changing field is discoverable, accessible, and reproducible.

![Image 11: PLOS Global Public Health](https://plos.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/Journal-Three-Column-Ribbon-470x235_Global-Public-Health.jpg)

### [PLOS Global Public Health](https://journals.plos.org/globalpublichealth/)

_PLOS Global Public Health_ makes interdisciplinary research of the highest ethical and methodological rigor visible and accessible to health professionals, policy-makers, and local communities, prioritizing diversity, equity, and inclusion in public health research. We welcome qualitative and quantitative primary research in a range of topics from maternal and child health, global health security, and evidence use and policy, to infectious and non-communicable diseases and environmental health.

![Image 12: PLOS Medicine](https://plos.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/Journal-Three-Column-Ribbon-470x235_Medicine.jpg)

### [PLOS Medicine](https://journals.plos.org/plosmedicine/)

_PLOS Medicine_ publishes high-impact research that transforms healthcare delivery, shapes policy, and advances clinical understanding. Our scope encompasses critical challenges in global health—from major diseases to health equity and the social determinants of health—with emphasis on work that bridges research and real-world implementation. The journal serves as a trusted platform where rigorous methodology meets practical impact, connecting researchers, healthcare professionals, and policymakers via collaborative editorial support to drive meaningful improvements in global health outcomes.

![Image 13: PLOS Mental Health](https://plos.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/Journal-Three-Column-Ribbon-470x235_Mental-Health.jpg)

### [PLOS Mental Health](https://journals.plos.org/mentalhealth/)

_PLOS Mental Health_ is a global, multidisciplinary journal that brings together research aimed at improving the mental health and well-being of all people around the world. Works published will range from academic and clinical research, to submissions on technology to support improved mental health, and policy and governance. Topics include, but are not restricted to, lived experience, community mental health, public mental health and policy, socio-economic and environmental impacts, psychiatry and occupational mental health.

![Image 14: PLOS Neglected Tropical Diseases](https://plos.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/Journal-Three-Column-Ribbon-470x235_Neglected-Tropical-Diseases.jpg)

### [PLOS Neglected Tropical Diseases](https://journals.plos.org/plosntds/)

_PLOS Neglected Tropical Diseases_ covers the epidemiology, pathology, treatment, prevention and control of neglected tropical diseases, defined as poverty-promoting infectious diseases that primarily occur in rural areas and poor urban areas of low-income and middle-income countries. Research in all aspects of these diseases is welcome, from clinical features to vector biology, public health, social sciences and policy.

![Image 15: PLOS One](https://plos.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/Journal-Three-Column-Ribbon-470x235_One.jpg)

We evaluate research on the basis of scientific validity, strong methodology, and high ethical standards, selecting for research that contributes to academic knowledge. We encourage inter-and multidisciplinary studies, and accept a range of submissions from primary research to protocols and systematic reviews, including research with negative or null results.

![Image 16: PLOS Water](https://plos.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/Journal-Three-Column-Ribbon-470x235_Water.jpg)

### [PLOS Water](https://journals.plos.org/water/)

_PLOS Water_ brings together research of the highest methodological and ethical standards for water as a vital resource for societies in every region of the world. Covering topics ranging from water access and security, to health impacts and behavioral research, the broad scope unites research across the interconnected issues of clean water supply and consumption, empowering researchers to drive collaboration in order to create real global change.

![Image 17: PLOS Climate](https://plos.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/Journal-Three-Column-Ribbon-470x235_Climate.jpg)

_PLOS Climate_ empowers global, multidisciplinary collaboration, and enables decision-makers at every level of society to take urgent, evidence-based action on the causes and impacts of climate change. Bringing together scientific research and analysis across disciplines generates powerful insights, which we share transparently and equitably to catalyze real progress.

### [PLOS Ecosystems](https://journals.plos.org/ecosystems/)

_PLOS Ecosystems_ is a multidisciplinary, open access journal that brings together research relevant to addressing the challenges facing our terrestrial, freshwater and marine ecosystems, and nature’s contributions to people. This selective journal is a forum for impactful research on the conservation, management, restoration, sustainability, and use of ecosystems across scales.

As our leading sustainability science journal, _PLOS Sustainability and Transformation_ brings together original research, addressing the global challenges of transitioning to a more sustainable and just future. # [Apply to join PLOS Climate's editorial board](https://survey.alchemer.com/s3/7201552/8a34bdb543de)

We are seeking Academic Editors across four new sections of the journal

### Editorial: Four years of PLOS Climate: Past, present and future

#### Our Editors-in-Chief and Executive Editor reflect on what our community has achieved so far and where we’re heading next

[Read](https://journals.plos.org/climate/article?id=10.1371/journal.pclm.0000866)

08/13/2026

Opinion

## [Using a “Super” El Niño to understand how lakes respond to climate extremes](https://journals.plos.org/climate/article?id=10.1371/journal.pclm.0001021)

Culpepper and colleagues highlight the opportunity to use the upcoming ‘super” El Niño to investigate the effects of climate variability on lakes.

Image credit: [Autumn](https://journals.plos.org/climate/%E2%80%9Chttps://pixabay.com/photos/autumn-nature-reflection-lake-8356402/%22) by Sukitha Udugamasooriya, [Pixabay License](https://pixabay.com/service/license/)

[![Image 2: Using a “Super” El Niño to understand how lakes respond to climate extremes](https://journals.plos.org/climate/indirect/60e7491d3c7c12497414b3ab0846906ea9ba879222bd2a1f6b91f7c3fb670e67)](https://journals.plos.org/climate/article?id=10.1371/journal.pclm.0001021)

08/06/2026

Review

## [Advances in regional climate science in South America and Central America during the CORDEX Era](https://journals.plos.org/climate/article?id=10.1371/journal.pclm.0001015)

Bettolli and colleagues review fifteen years of progress in regional climate modelling in South and Central America.

Image credit: [Volcano](https://journals.plos.org/climate/%E2%80%9Chttps://pixabay.com/photos/volcano-nicaragua-concepcion-2259249/%22) by Praesentator, [Pixabay License](https://pixabay.com/service/license/)

[![Image 3: Advances in regional climate science in South America and Central America during the CORDEX Era](https://journals.plos.org/climate/indirect/24756e432e140f496997847093779d2875df3d4e28908f61b8fcad7654898f56)](https://journals.plos.org/climate/article?id=10.1371/journal.pclm.0001015)

07/28/2026

Research Article

## [Communicating uncertainty to policy makers in maps: A systematic scoping review of meaningful to misleading current practice](https://journals.plos.org/climate/article?id=10.1371/journal.pclm.0000707)

Jain and colleagues identify an urgent need to improve current practice in the visual communication of uncertainty to support informed, considered policy and planning relating to climate-related infectious disease.

Image credit: [Coins](https://journals.plos.org/climate/%E2%80%9Chttps://pixabay.com/photos/hand-out-meeting-meeting-room-4551066/%22) by hamcos-IT, [Pixabay License](https://pixabay.com/service/license/)

[![Image 4: Communicating uncertainty to policy makers in maps: A systematic scoping review of meaningful to misleading current practice](https://journals.plos.org/climate/indirect/0f2324de19e00616a45943746bc3148658ceef65ec277addfb62a1d2fa05c3c1)](https://journals.plos.org/climate/article?id=10.1371/journal.pclm.0000707)

07/23/2026

Essay

## [All climate models are wrong but wrong models are useful: Why, where, and how?](https://journals.plos.org/climate/article?id=10.1371/journal.pclm.0001000)

Douville argues that recognizing that all ESMs are imperfect could allow us to use them more wisely, at a lower cost, and with greater efficiency.

Image credit: [Puzzle](https://journals.plos.org/climate/%E2%80%9Chttps://pixabay.com/photos/puzzle-pieces-puzzle-share-game-7696621/%22) by congerdesign, [Pixabay License](https://pixabay.com/service/license/)

[![Image 5: All climate models are wrong but wrong models are useful: Why, where, and how?](https://journals.plos.org/climate/indirect/0e55389c38e0ac45c448c6e5eef1f3d9162c548288b841e588c8de214ffefbe3)](https://journals.plos.org/climate/article?id=10.1371/journal.pclm.0001000)

08/12/2026

Research Article

## [Mapping climate-related forest risks: An index-based approach](https://journals.plos.org/climate/article?id=10.1371/journal.pclm.0000931)

Martes and Köhl explore climate risks to Germany's forests and opportunities to increase their resilience.

[![Image 6: Mapping climate-related forest risks: An index-based approach](https://journals.plos.org/climate/indirect/213d7fc516eb9d413b5098d893d4a7de5c4dfe3bd5705a94f2c465b83844edaa)](https://journals.plos.org/climate/article?id=10.1371/journal.pclm.0000931)
Image credit: [Black Forest](https://journals.plos.org/climate/%E2%80%9Chttps://pixabay.com/photos/black-forest-fog-clouds-mystical-1476021/%22) by Thomas Wolter, [Pixabay License](https://pixabay.com/service/license/)

08/05/2026

Research Article

## [The inflationary effects of the El Niño-Southern Oscillation](https://journals.plos.org/climate/article?id=10.1371/journal.pclm.0000985)

Gallegati and colleagues explore the complexities of the impacts of the ENSO cycle and ENSO diversity on national inflation rates.

[![Image 7: The inflationary effects of the El Niño-Southern Oscillation](https://journals.plos.org/climate/indirect/163b3babf378fe05299cc4e40e0fd7e126961312cb99ce92b1ebacdb1bde1b37)](https://journals.plos.org/climate/article?id=10.1371/journal.pclm.0000985)
Image credit: [Coins](https://journals.plos.org/climate/%E2%80%9Chttps://pixabay.com/photos/coins-money-profit-savings-stack-18134/%22) by PublicDomainPictures, [Pixabay License](https://pixabay.com/service/license/)

07/16/2026

Research Article

## [Accuracy, robustness and comprehensibility – Challenges in bottom-up energy system models](https://journals.plos.org/climate/article?id=10.1371/journal.pclm.0000890)

Prina and Noussan provide a roadmap of the challenges facing energy system models, equipping the field with a clearer path to close the gap between modelling results and the concrete requirements of energy policy development and energy transition implementation.

[![Image 8: Accuracy, robustness and comprehensibility – Challenges in bottom-up energy system models](https://journals.plos.org/climate/indirect/86a28a0f4ab2bdb42b79cc43eec56be26c1a6bb1cd5ccaa61bf521292fd10b84)](https://journals.plos.org/climate/article?id=10.1371/journal.pclm.0000890)
Image credit: [Power](https://journals.plos.org/climate/%E2%80%9Chttps://pixabay.com/photos/power-pole-power-line-high-voltage-6903947/%22) by Terranaut, [Pixabay License](https://pixabay.com/service/license/)

07/20/2026

Research Article

## [Statistical learning for climate-GDP panels: Data cleaning, flexible trend controls, and predictive validation](https://journals.plos.org/climate/article?id=10.1371/journal.pclm.0000962)

Schötz and colleagues reveal that widely used models and predictors in climate econometrics have little out-of-sample predictive power.

[![Image 9: Statistical learning for climate-GDP panels: Data cleaning, flexible trend controls, and predictive validation](https://journals.plos.org/climate/indirect/a2780ea723160920ea137e65ebb96bd6b56f13f250ff8dd922d4dffa2db186fa)](https://journals.plos.org/climate/article?id=10.1371/journal.pclm.0000962)
Image credit: [Euro](https://journals.plos.org/climate/%E2%80%9Chttps://pixabay.com/photos/euro-coins-currency-cent-euro-cent-1353420/%22) by image4you, [Pixabay License](https://pixabay.com/service/license/)

07/10/2026

Research Article

## [Dynamic health risks of sudden temperature drops in subtropical winter time: A case study in Hong Kong](https://journals.plos.org/climate/article?id=10.1371/journal.pclm.0000980)

Wang and colleagues find that abrupt shifts in temperature, made more likely by climate change, significantly increase mortality risk among older people in Hong Kong.

[![Image 10: Dynamic health risks of sudden temperature drops in subtropical winter time: A case study in Hong Kong](https://journals.plos.org/climate/indirect/dbc60d082646b14f0ca5d53317833742bf3637b978a603525974a6bf5c91f4aa)](https://journals.plos.org/climate/article?id=10.1371/journal.pclm.0000980)
Image credit: [Hong Kong](https://journals.plos.org/climate/%E2%80%9Chttps://pixabay.com/photos/hong-kong-victoria-harbour-hongkong-4370342/%22) by Steven Yu, [Pixabay License](https://pixabay.com/service/license/)

07/14/2026

Research Article

## [AI-assisted longitudinal comparison of scenario knowledge representation in IPCC synthesis reports](https://journals.plos.org/climate/article?id=10.1371/journal.pclm.0000965)

Warin and Bisson show that the six IPCC synthesis reports exhibit both continuity and transformation in their answers to identical scenario-based prompts.

[![Image 11: AI-assisted longitudinal comparison of scenario knowledge representation in IPCC synthesis reports](https://journals.plos.org/climate/indirect/1475fb3c4166ff63013ddb392556cad84c54872377c5399116636f67e18740a0)](https://journals.plos.org/climate/article?id=10.1371/journal.pclm.0000965)
Image credit: [Clouds](https://journals.plos.org/climate/%E2%80%9Chttps://pixabay.com/photos/clouds-heaven-weather-5348740/%22) by Tama66, [Pixabay License](https://pixabay.com/service/license/)

07/07/2026

Research Article

## [Finding the sea level – Investigation of rural references for estimation of the urban heat island](https://journals.plos.org/climate/article?id=10.1371/journal.pclm.0000955)

Kittner and colleagues demonstrate the potential of ERA5-Land reanalysis data as a rural reference in urban heat island calculations.

[![Image 12: Finding the sea level – Investigation of rural references for estimation of the urban heat island](https://journals.plos.org/climate/indirect/8ea2cd3232b9048b62be0bb530d04bbe39139f42fa5fbf991815ab23d4cbaf5a)](https://journals.plos.org/climate/article?id=10.1371/journal.pclm.0000955)
Image credit: [Berlin](https://journals.plos.org/climate/%E2%80%9Chttps://pixabay.com/photos/berlin-television-tower-skyline-4001319/%22) by Kranich17, [Pixabay License](https://pixabay.com/service/license/)

# PMC Collections

## Abstract

[](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462)
The origins of money and the formulation of coherent weight and measurement systems are amongst the most significant prehistoric developments of the human intellect. We present a method for detecting perceptible standardization of weights and apply this to 5028 Early Bronze Age rings, ribs, and axe blades from Central Europe. We calculate the degree of uniformity on the basis of psychophysics, and quantify this using similarity indexes. The analysis shows that 70.3% of all rings could not be perceptibly distinguished from a ring weighing 195.5 grams, indicating their suitability as commodity money. Perceptive weight equivalence is demonstrated between rings, and a selection of ribs and axe blades. Co-occurrence of these objects evidences their interchangeability. We further suggest that producing copies of rings led to recognition of weight similarities and the independent emergence of a system of weighing in Central Europe at the end of the Early Bronze Age.

[](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462 "Introduction")
## Introduction

[](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462)
Money is a type of commodity that acts as a means of exchange and is standardized to some degree, visually or in terms of their weight [[1](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref001), [2](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref002)]. Archaeology can provide a unique perspective on the development of money and systems of weighing over space and time, but the discipline has difficulties with the identification of objects that functioned either as commodity money or as (balance) weights. Typical statistical approaches are inadequate for dealing with the approximation that characterizes prehistoric weighing [[3](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref003), [4](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref004)]. What is needed for archaeology to contribute to the history of metrology and the origins of money are methods for identifying standardization on the basis of perceived similarity. A principal challenge at this point is to take the statistical tools employed to express accuracy, and adjust them in accordance to the findings from psychophysics, so that the ordinal and qualitative measurements of weight estimation by hand and sight are taken on board. In short, prehistoric weight units quite literally need to make sense.

[](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462 "Bronze Age commodities")
### Bronze Age commodities

[](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462)
Commodities are archaeologically defined as socially recognized, alienable objects that appear in large numbers and emphasize similarity [[5](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref005)–[9](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref009)]. Candidates of prehistoric commodity money from the Central European Early Bronze Age are the so-called _Ösenringe_ (hereafter rings), _Spangenbarren_ (hereafter ribs), and possibly axe blades. Rings and ribs appear in the southern parts of Central Europe: the Danubian region of southern Germany, Lower Austria, and parts of the Czech Republic. Axe blades are typically, but not exclusively, found in central and north-eastern Germany, roughly corresponding to the cultural area of the Únětice. In between is an area of overlap where rings, ribs, and axe blades are regularly found together, primarily the Czech Republic (Moravia and Bohemia), though some mixed hoards also appear in north-eastern Germany and Poland ([Fig 1](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone-0240462-g001)). A third geographical region where these objects are encountered is Southern Scandinavia, though in lesser numbers [[10](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref010)] ([S1A Appendix](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.s001)).

[](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462)

[![Image 13: thumbnail](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article/figure/image?size=inline&id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462.g001)](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article/figure/image?size=medium&id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462.g001 "Click for larger image")

*   [TIFF original image](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article/figure/image?download&size=original&id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462.g001)

Fig 1.  Map of Central Europe with the hoards used in this study.

[](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462)

Includes drawings of objects after Stein [[11](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref011)] (made with Natural Earth).

[https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0240462.g001](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0240462.g001)

[](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462)
It is generally thought that different economies operated in the three regions where rings, ribs, and axe blades occur [[10](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref010)]. In the southern region commodification was strongest and the economy is often interpreted as resembling to some degree a market economy, in which rings and ribs represented wealth [[12](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref012)–[15](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref015)]. The Únětice region is better characterized as prestige-good exchange, though some commodification is visible [[14](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref014)]. Scandinavia is different altogether. Here the context of rings suggests gift-exchange, and they mostly appear deposited as single finds in wetlands [[10](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref010)]. A clear contrast between gift and market economies seems hard to sustain, however, and may be little more than a modern distinction [[5](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref005), [10](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref010), [16](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref016)].

[](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462)
Found in bulk, sometimes in hoards containing multiple hundreds, many of the rings, ribs and axe blades are considered to have no other practical function besides their tentative use as ingots, or rough-outs for further production [[8](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref008), [17](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref017)–[23](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref023)]. Moulds, made of clay, stone, or casted directly in sand [[24](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref024)], made serial production possible, which led to some degree of unintentional standardization. However, there are indications that for some types of objects a deliberate effort was made to achieve a specific weight interval, meaning that weight mattered ([S1A Appendix](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.s001)). In the case of rings, a standardization between roughly 170 and 220 grams has been hypothesized on the basis of histograms [[17](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref017)–[19](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref019)]. Unclear is how prehistoric people would have recognized this standard.

[](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462 "Psychophysics of weight discrimination")
### Psychophysics of weight discrimination

[](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462)
The practice of weighing may have been far more imprecise than is generally assumed. According to Gyllenbok [[25](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref025)], historically there are three basic ways to measure weight: 1) Through lifting two objects and comparing them, or estimation on sight. 2) Through practicality, i.e. the maximum weight that could be conveniently carried by a human or animal. 3) By means of a weighing apparatus. Each of these have their own level of impreciseness.

[](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462)
In the case of the Central European Early Bronze Age, there is no evidence of a weighing apparatus such as balances. Weighing was a qualitative measurement based on comparative sensory perception with hands and eyes. But humans are known to be “rather ‘noisy’ measurement instruments” [[26](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref026)]. Prehistoric standardization thus would have been imprecise, and worked based on approximation both in shape and weight. They must have had relatively low precision in terms of modern scientific tolerances [[25](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref025)] and this should be taken into consideration when looking for standardization.

[](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462)
We assume that in the absence of measuring equipment counting must have been the preferred method of quantification, but the counted objects had to be perceptibly similar [[25](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref025), [27](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref027), [28](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref028)]. Therefore, weight mattered. Weight is crucial for the determination of the value of goods in most economic transactions [[3](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref003)]. Lacking balances, the only way to observe a reasonable degree of uniformity is through sensory perception. We consider objects uniform when they are perceptibly indiscriminate from each other.

[](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462)
Psychophysics offers a methodology through which we can test the perceptible similarity of objects based on weight. This sub-field of cognitive psychology is concerned with the relationships between physical properties of stimuli and perceptual responses to these stimuli [[29](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref029)–[31](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref031)]. The measure used to express people’s sensory acuity is the Weber fraction, and denotes the difference in stimulus strength that is just noticeable. As a general rule, the Weber fraction for weight discrimination is 0.1 [[32](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref032)–[34](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref034)]. This means that the difference between, for example, a weight of 100 grams and 105 grams is not noticeable, but between 100 and 111 grams is, since the threshold is at 110 grams ([Methods](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#sec011)).

[](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462 "Data")
### Data

[](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462)
Using the measurement of weight, we employ a methodology based on psychophysics to quantify and operationalize our assumption that weighing in prehistory was a purely sensorial practice, done by hand. The perceptive equivalence is expressed though the calculation of a similarity index (SI), which gives the percentage of objects from a dataset that are perceptibly indistinguishable from a tested object ([Methods](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#sec011)).

[](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462)
We collected the weights of 6317 objects, of which 5028 were used in the analysis as they were complete and dated to the Early Bronze Age: 2639 rings, 1780 ribs, and 609 axe blades ([S2](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.s002) and [S3](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.s003) Appendices). Axe blades can be divided into Early Bronze I (hereafter: EBA I: 2150–1900 BCE) and Early Bronze Age II (hereafter EBA II: 1900–1700 BCE) on typological grounds [[35](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref035), [36](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref036)]. Rings and ribs mostly overlap, though ribs are generally considered a slightly later development [[18](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref018)].

[](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462)
We selected hoards originally containing at least five or more rings and ribs, or at least five axe blades ([S1C Appendix](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.s001)). This selection procedure helps identify standardized commodities rather than particular types of rings and axe blades ([S1B Appendix](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.s001)). We chose to draw the limit at five because we observed that rings and ribs are found in several instances in bundles of five [[17](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone.0240462.ref017)].

## Results

[](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462 "Rings and ribs")
### Rings and ribs

[](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462)
The analysis of the full dataset of rings and ribs revealed the existence of a peak at 193 grams, with a similarity index of 58.6% ([Fig 2A](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone-0240462-g002)). What this means is that when compared to a ring of 193 grams, nearly 60% of all other rings in the database are perceptibly similar in weight. When the dataset was broken into its two main components of rings and ribs, the following picture emerged. The rings, totaling 2639 objects, presented one peak with a similarity index of 70.3% at 195.5 grams ([Fig 2B](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone-0240462-g002)). The 1780 ribs had two peaks. One that corresponded largely with that of the rings, and stood at 186 grams and a similarity index of 44.3%, and a smaller one at 82 grams, having a similarity index of 13.1% ([Fig 2C](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone-0240462-g002)). The separation between the two peaks was estimated using clustering at 135 grams. This value was used to further separate the ribs into a group of heavier and one of lighter objects, which were then analyzed separately. The heavier ribs (n = 1106) revealed the existence of a comparable peak at 185.5 grams, where the similarity index rose to 71.5%. The lighter ribs showed a peak at 81 grams, though the similarity index only reached a maximum of 37.8% ([Fig 2D](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0240462#pone-0240462-g002)).
